title: UP RERA Bars Blanket Consent, Requires Two-Thirds Allottee Sign-Off Before Any Building Plan Change
seo_title: UP RERA: No Blanket Consent For Plan Changes
meta_description: UP RERA directs developers to disclose exact changes in writing and get two-thirds allottee consent under Section 14 before revising sanctioned plans.
court: Uttar Pradesh Real Estate Regulatory Authority (UP RERA)
case_name: UP RERA directive on consent for modification of sanctioned building plans
citation: UP RERA directive reported from around 12 November 2026, issued under Section 14 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016; UP RERA's own order or circular number not confirmed in available reports
body: Homebuyers in Uttar Pradesh's real estate projects, including the large townships ringing Noida and Greater Noida, have one more layer of protection against developers quietly reworking a sanctioned building plan after flats have already been sold. The Uttar Pradesh Real Estate Regulatory Authority has directed that promoters cannot seek a general or blanket consent from allottees before changing an approved plan; they must first set out the exact modifications in writing and then obtain dated, written consent from at least two-thirds of the allottees before the authority will even consider the application.

The trigger for the directive, as reported, was UP RERA's own experience processing applications: developers had been approaching the authority for approval of revised building plans while relying on consent documents that were either missing the specifics of what was changing or worded broadly enough to cover changes the allottees had not been told about in detail. A signature taken once, in general terms, was being treated by some promoters as good enough cover for whatever later change the project might need. UP RERA's directive closes that route.

Section 14 of the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 is the legal anchor for the two-thirds threshold, which restricts a promoter's ability to make structural changes or additions to a sanctioned plan, layout plan or specifications of a building, or to the common areas, without the written consent of a prescribed proportion of allottees. UP RERA's directive operationalises that threshold for the applications that reach it, insisting on dated consent from at least two-thirds of allottees in a project and requiring that the consent documents be filed along with the application seeking the plan revision, rather than produced only if challenged later.

Disclosing the full details of a proposed change in writing before seeking consent is the part most likely to change how developers actually operate on the ground. A promoter can no longer circulate a short form asking allottees to agree, in general terms, to 'modifications as may be required' and treat the resulting signatures as valid consent for a specific later change, such as reducing a clubhouse's size, adding floors within the same footprint, or altering a tower's layout. Each proposed change now needs to be spelled out before the clock starts on collecting signatures, and the application to the authority must show that the allottees who signed were shown that specific change, not a generic one.

For homebuyers, many of whom are high-net-worth individuals and families who have put significant sums into under-construction apartments in the National Capital Region on the strength of a particular approved plan, the directive gives a concrete basis to resist a developer's attempt to treat an old, general consent form as covering a new change years later. An allottee can point to the absence of a specific, dated consent addressing the exact modification in question and argue that the developer has not met the Section 14 threshold, regardless of what a broader form signed at booking may have said.

Developers active in Uttar Pradesh's real estate market face procedural discipline rather than a new substantive restriction: Section 14 consent was always required, but the directive removes the ambiguity that let some promoters treat a vague, earlier-collected consent as sufficient. Projects currently seeking UP RERA approval for a plan revision, including the stalled and restructured projects in Noida and Greater Noida that have been working through delay and resolution processes this year, will need fresh, specific, two-thirds consent on file before the authority takes up their application, adding a step that could slow approvals for promoters who had not already lined up proper documentation.

Family offices and resident Indian or overseas buyers who hold multiple units in a single large township project, a common pattern among high-net-worth purchasers buying for investment rather than occupation, stand to gain the most leverage from the clearer threshold. Where a project has hundreds of allottees spread across phases, assembling genuine two-thirds consent on a specifically disclosed change is a materially harder task for a promoter than collecting signatures on a generic form at the time of booking, which gives organised groups of allottees, including larger investors with several units, more practical say over whether a plan change actually goes through.
why_it_matters: A building plan change made after allottees have booked and paid for flats can affect everything from the size of common amenities to the view from a particular tower, and Section 14 of RERA already required allottee consent for such changes. UP RERA's directive removes the room developers had to rely on vague, general consent forms, insisting instead on specific written disclosure of the exact change followed by dated consent from at least two-thirds of allottees, which gives homebuyers in Noida, Greater Noida and across Uttar Pradesh a sharper tool to challenge plan changes made without proper sign-off.
card_summary: UP RERA has directed developers to disclose exact plan changes in writing and obtain dated, two-thirds allottee consent before seeking approval to revise a sanctioned building plan.
card_tip: A general consent signed at booking, without specifics of the later change, does not satisfy Section 14; allottees can demand dated consent to the exact modification before a plan is revised.
verification_notes: The core elements of the directive, the ban on blanket or general consent, the requirement that developers disclose the specific proposed change in writing before seeking consent, the two-thirds allottee consent threshold, the requirement that consent documents be dated and filed with the application, and the link to Section 14 of RERA, are confirmed consistently across four independently published reports: Outlook Money, Constro Facilitator, Aurum PropTech and The CSR Journal, all dated around 12 to 13 November 2026. None of these reports gave an official order or circular number for the directive, nor did any of them reproduce the original UP RERA document, so this draft does not state one and flags that gap in the citation field rather than inventing a number. The trigger described, developers filing applications with inadequate or overly general consent, is drawn from the same set of reports and is consistent across them. No specific project or developer is named in connection with this directive in any source checked, so none is named here.
